decision.about: What server should the revived watcher check pages against, now that its old default (port 8123) is not running?

options.say: Point HEALTH_BASE at http://localhost:80, the owner's own live server, read-only
options.why: it is the exact server that actually broke three times tonight -- checking a copy proves nothing about the real thing; the watcher only ever sends a handful of debounced GET page-loads (capped at 8 per batch already), the same kind of read a browser tab makes, no writes, no state change; and it costs nothing extra to start -- no second whole Express+supervisor process idling for a watcher whose own header brags about near-zero CPU while nothing changes

options.say: Start a dedicated private server on a free 809x port and point the watcher at that
options.why: fully isolates any load from the owner's server -- but it tests a SEPARATE copy of the site (its own directory.json, its own in-memory state), so it could read clean while the owner's real :80 is the one actually broken, which defeats the point; it also means running and supervising a second full server process just to have something to watch

decision.because: The brief itself flags this as probably the safer, lighter choice, and it is: read-only GETs against the real live server, capped and debounced, versus a whole second server process to babysit. If load ever becomes a real concern the fix is a one-line HEALTH_BASE env override, not a redesign.

decision.about: How should the revived watcher be kept alive, given the fence rules out editing Server/server.js and health.mjs must stay killable independently of the dev server?

options.say: Server/health-supervisor.mjs: a small new file that forks health.mjs as a child, restarts it on exit (with backoff if it dies fast, straight back if it had genuinely been running), and a watchdog backstop -- the same fork/restart/bounded-kill shape server.js already proved for the dev server, minus the HTTP boot-test half (health.mjs opens no port, so there is nothing to poll for a 200)
options.why: reuses the proven mechanism instead of inventing a second one, without sharing server.js's own process -- health.mjs's own header promises it can be killed any time with nothing else noticing, which a shared supervisor would break

options.say: Add health.mjs as a second child server.js's own supervisor manages
options.why: one supervisor instead of two -- rejected outright: this task's fence explicitly forbids editing Server/server.js

options.say: Hand it to the idle pm2 daemon already on this machine, or a Windows service
options.why: a real process manager with restart policies built in -- rejected for tonight: no npm dependency / no new always-on infra was decided without asking first, and the brief's own note says the existing pm2 daemon is on the owner's own list, not mine to adopt mid-task

decision.because: matches the fence, reuses the already-proven mechanism, and keeps health.mjs's own kill-anytime promise intact.

log.msg: PROVED end to end on a live run: started `node Server/health-supervisor.mjs` -- it forked health.mjs (pid 33552), which booted against http://localhost:80 as decided, and wrote public/framework/ai/health/heartbeat.json (supervisor_pid 10492, child_pid 33552, restarts 0). Then killed the health.mjs child directly with `taskkill /PID 33552 /F` -- the exact 'someone kills it' scenario this task exists to fix. Within about 3 seconds the supervisor logged the exit (code 1) and forked a fresh child (pid 36672); heartbeat.json updated to restarts: 1 with the new child_pid. This is the watcher surviving being killed, proved, not assumed.

PROVED the actual break-detection end to end, safely: built public/framework/ai/2026-09-19/health-revive/scratch-break/ (a disposable page under this task's own folder, declared as this task's own child so it is routable but linked from nowhere else). Confirmed clean first (screenshot + a clean watcher pass, no findings). Edited it to call a method that does not exist -- health.mjs caught it within seconds: {"error":{"url":"/framework/ai/2026-09-19/health-revive/scratch-break/","kind":"console","text":"TypeError: this.deliberately_missing_method is not a function..."}} (public/framework/ai/health/2026-09-19.jsonl line 874). Screenshotted the real broken page (Page Load Error, the exact message) -- saved as proof-broken.png in this task dir and shown on this task's own page.js. Then fixed it back -- health.mjs logged {"ok":{"url":".../scratch-break/"}} 39 seconds later (line 883). UNPROMPTED BONUS PROOF: the very next edit I made (fixing the break) was blocked by the real PostToolUse hook, health-guard.mjs, telling me plainly I had broken that exact page 36 seconds earlier -- proving the whole pipeline (watcher -> log -> hook -> the editing agent) is alive end to end, not just the watcher in isolation. This is proven, not assumed -- no page the owner uses was ever touched.

Supervision proven a second way: after the break/fix test, restarted health-supervisor.mjs cleanly, then killed its health.mjs child with taskkill /F a second time -- confirmed via heartbeat.json restarts count incrementing again and a fresh child_pid appearing within seconds. Then killed the SUPERVISOR itself with taskkill /F (no /T) mid-test -- confirmed its health.mjs child (pid 36672) exited on its own (fork()'s IPC channel closing), so no orphan was left; verified with tasklist. Started the real, final instance detached via PowerShell Start-Process -WindowStyle Hidden (not tied to this session's own shell) -- supervisor pid 34636, watcher child pid 34924, both confirmed alive via tasklist and heartbeat.json after this task's own tool session moved on to other work. To stop it later: read supervisor_pid from public/framework/ai/health/heartbeat.json and kill that pid (killing only the child pid gets it restarted -- that is the point).

assign.outcome: **`Server/health.mjs` is alive again, supervised, and proven to catch a real break.** It was found dead tonight — no process, nothing that would ever restart it, watching a server (`:8123`) that wasn't even running, and its findings page linked from nowhere. Findings and live-alive status are now on today's AI board: [Health, revived](/framework/ai/2026-09-19/health-revive/).
